title: Adrenal glands – high-yield summary
html:
Source: Adrenal Glands High-Yield Summary.pdf – 12 pages

Adrenal Glands: High-Yield Summary #1

  • 1. Core Anatomy & Physiology
  • The Adrenal Gland is composed of 2 distinct functional units:
  • ☆ Medulla: Chromaffin cells, secretes CATECHOLAMINES (80% Epinephrine, 20% Norepi) directly into the bloodstream.
  • ☆ Cortex: 3 distinct zones with different functions and regulators.
  • - Zona Glomerulosa (Outer) => ALDOSTERONE
  • Key Regulator: Renin-Angiotensin System (and K+)
  • - Zona Fasciculata (Middle) => CORTISOL
  • Key Regulator: ACTH
  • - Zona Reticularis (Inner) => Adrenal ANDROGENS (DHEA, Androstenedione)
  • Key Regulator: ACTH
  • ⚠️Crucial enzyme distinction:
  • Glomerulosa cannot synthesize cortisol because it lacks 17α-hydroxylase.
  • Fasciculata/Reticularis cannot synthesize aldosterone because they lack CYP11B2 (P450aldo)
  • 2. Regulation of:
  • CORTISOL secretion (3 MECHANISMS)
  • 1) Circadian rhythm + Episodic secretion
  • LOWEST at midnight (12:00-1:00 might be undetectable); SURGE starts at 3rd-5th h but max during 6th-8th hour of sleep
  • Declines during the day: values obtained later are lower and are approximately half of morning values, at 4 p.m.
  • 2) Stress responsiveness of the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis
  • Surgery, hypoglycemia →CNS → ↑ CRH → ↑ ACTH → ↑ Cortisol
  • 3) Negative feedback inhibition
  • By glucocorticoids, of CRH, ACTH, & Cortisol secretion
  • ADRENAL ANDROGENS: Regulated by ACTH but NO feedback inhibition on ACTH
  • Their direct biologic activity (androstenedione, DHEA, and DHEA sulfate) = minimal as they function primarily as precursors for peripheral
  • conversion to the active androgenic hormones, testosterone, and dihydrotestosterone.
  • Thus, DHEA sulfate undergoes limited conversion to DHEA, which can be further converted in peripheral tissues to androstenedione, the immediate
  • precursor of the active androgens.
  • ALDOSTERONE: Primarily regulated by RAAS & K+, NOT ACTH
  • 3. PRIMARY ADRENOCORTICAL INSUFFICIENCY (ADDISON'S DISEASE)
  • Deficient adrenal production of glucocorticoids and/or mineralocorticoids.
  • ● Etiologies:

☆ APS Type 1 or Autoimmune PolyEndocrinopathy, Candidiasis, & Ectodermal Dystrophy (APECED #2

  • Autosomal recessive, AIRE gene mutation (chr 21) w/ childhood onset
  • => HypoPTH, chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, ACI, gonadal failure, Hypothyroidism, DMT1, DI + alopecia, B12 anemia,
  • chronic active hepatitis
  • • Autoantibodies: Anti-P450scc (CYP11A1)
  • ☆ APS Type 2 (Schmidt's syndrome):
  • Adult onset, Polygenic, HLA-DR3/CTLA4 association
  • => ACI, Autoimmune thyroid disease, gonadal failure, DMT1, vitiligo, B12 anemia
  • • Autoantibodies: Anti-21-hydroxylase (P450c21, CYP21A2)
  • ● Clinical Features of Primary ACI:
  • ☆ Hyperpigmentation (classic, earliest sign) in: sun-exposed areas, pressure points (knuckles, elbows, knees), buccal
  • mucosa, gums, palmar creases, nail beds, scars (newer scars hyperpigment)
  • - Weakness, fatigue, malaise, anorexia, weight loss (up to 15 kg)
  • ☆ Cardiovascular: Hypotension (90%), orthostatic dizziness, positive Schellong test (↓ in BP within 3 min of standing)
  • - GI: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea/constipation, abdominal pain
  • ☆ Salt craving (20%), Hypoglycemia (<<< secondary ACI & children)
  • - Loss of axillary/pubic hair in females (↓ adrenal androgens)
  • - Vitiligo (4-17% of autoimmune cases)
  • DDX w/ Secondary adrenal insufficiency:
  • NO hyperpigmentat° (PALE = WHITE Addison's) & Mineralocorticoid secret° = usually normal (no hyperK+ or salt wasting)
  • ● DIAGNOSIS of Primary ACI
  • ○ STEP 1 (Asses the function of the adrenal cortex and confirm adrenal insufficiency):
  • NV Cortisol: 8 a.m =5–25 μg/dL -> 6-8 p.m =2.5–13.0 μg/dL (half) -> 12 a.m = <7 μg/dL
  • TEST DIAG = Paired 8-9AM measurement of Serum Cortisol + Plasma ACTH
  • ☆ Undetectable serum cortisol + elevated ACTH = PAI but if Cortisol > 550 nmol/L (20 µg/dL) = excludes diagnosis
  • ☆ Rapid ACTH Stimulation Test w/ a cosyntropin (Synacthen):
  • ○ Give 0.25 mg IM/IV of cosyntropin and measure cortisol at 30-60 min
  • ○ Peak < 500 nmol/L = diagnostic of PAI (also overt secondary)
  • ○ Peak > 550 nmol/L = Normal response (excludes PAI and overt secondary)
  • NOTE: Normal response does NOT rule out partial ACTH deficiency or recent secondary ACI
  • Plasma ACTH interpretation:
  • ☆ Primary ACI: ACTH HIGH vs. Secondary ACI: ACTH LOW or inappropriately normal (< 10 pg/mL)
  • Additional labs in ACI:
  • ☆ Hyponatremia + Hyperkalemia (classic)
  • ☆ Normocytic normochromic anemia (↓ androgens) w/ neutropenia, eosinophilia, lymphocytosis
  • ☆ ↑ BUN/Creatinine (volume depletion)
  • ☆ Hypoglycemia (< 70 mg/dL)
  • • Mild acidosis, mild hypercalcemia
  • • ECG: Low voltage, vertical QRS axis, nonspecific ST-T changes
  • ○ STEP 2 (Establish the etiology):
  • ☆ Adrenal autoantibodies (Anti-21-hydroxylase, Anti-17-hydroxylase, Anti P450 scc & Adrenal cortex antibodies (ACA))
  • ☆ CT Abdomen:
  • → Enlarged/calcified (or not) adrenals → TB, infiltration, metastases
  • → Small/atrophic adrenals → Chronic autoimmune adrenalitis
  • • CT-guided biopsy if metastases suspected

● TREATMENT of chronic ACI: #3

  • Glucocorticoid replacement: ☆ Hydrocortisone 15-25 mg/day=> Ex: 10 mg on waking, 5 mg midday, 5 mg 4-5 PM
  • Alternative = Prednisone 5 - 7.5 mg/day
  • Mineralocorticoid replacement: ☆ Fludrocortisone 0.05 - 0.2 mg/day (Not usually needed in secondary ACI)
  • Rmq: 40 mg HC = mineralocorticoid effect of 100 µg fludrocortisone
  • DHEA replacement: ☆ 25-50 mg/day may improve mood, well-being & libido in women
  • - Lifestyle: increase protein, vitamins & adequate sodium intake (NO restriction of sodium!!!⚠️)
  • - Monitoring:
  • Clinical: Resolution of weakness, fatigue, GI symptoms; hyperpigmentation improves
  • OVERtreatment => Cushingoid features, weight gain, hypertension, edema
  • UNDERtreatment => Persistent sx, postural hypotension, salt craving
  • Biochemical: Serum electrolytes, Plasma Renin (elevated if fludrocortisone insufficient)
  • - Prevention of adrenal crisis (pt education):
  • ☆ NEVER miss a dose
  • ☆ Minor stress: DOUBLE or triple HC dose (eg. Febrile illness)
  • ☆ Major stress (surgery): Increase up to 200-400 mg HC/day
  • ☆ If vomiting and can’t take the tb → seek immediate medical attention
  • • Wear MedicAlert/SOS bracelet + Steroid card
  • 4. ACUTE ADRENOCORTICAL INSUFFICIENCY (ADDISONIAN CRISIS)
  • Acute adrenocortical insufficiency triggered by stress (infection, trauma, surgery, dehydration, vomiting, diarrhea).
  • ● Clinical picture:
  • ☆ Hypotension + Shock + Volume depletion, dehydration + Fever (infection)
  • • Weakness, apathy, depressed mentation
  • • Abdominal pain (can mimic acute surgical abdomen) - LESS frequent
  • • Nausea, vomiting, anorexia, muscle cramps,
  • ☆ Hypoglycemia
  • ⚠️ Shock and coma can rapidly lead to death if untreated
  • ● Labs:
  • ☆ Hyponatremia, Hyperkalemia
  • ☆ Hypoglycemia
  • ☆ ↑ Urea, ↑ Creatinine, ↑ Ht
  • ☆ Metabolic acidosis
  • ☆ ↓ CORTISOL (confirmatory)
  • ☆ Lymphocytosis, Eosinophilia
  • ● Management (EMERGENCY):
  • 1. Take blood for glucose, electrolytes, urea, creatinine, cortisol BEFORE treatment
  • 2. DO NOT wait for results if clinical suspicion is high
  • 3. IV 0.9% Saline + 5% Glucose (correct volume and hypoglycemia)
  • 4. IV Hydrocortisone: 100 mg IV stat → 50-75 mg every 6 hours
  • - When stable: reduce to 50 mg every 6 hours
  • - Taper to maintenance by day 4-5
  • 5. Mineralocorticoid NOT needed acutely (high-dose HC + IV fluids provide enough mineralocorticoid effect)
  • 6. Identify and treat precipitating cause (e.g., infection)

5. CONGENITAL ADRENAL HYPERPLASIA (CAH) #4

  • Group of inherited disorders characterized by a deficiency of one of the enzymes necessary for cortisol biosynthesis.
  • In many cases, CAH results in lack of cortisol + overproduction of androgen
  • >90% d/t 21α-hydroxylase deficiency
  • ● Pathophysiology (21-OH Deficiency):
  • Cortisol + Aldosterone def. → Loss of (-) feedback → ACTH hypersecretion→Adrenal hyperplasia + Accumulation of
  • precursors (17OHP, Progesterone)→ Shunting to androgen pathways → ↑ Testosterone, Androstenedione, DHT
  • ● Clinical picture = csq of the degree of enzymatic deficiency
  • From presentation in neonatal period w/ salt wasting and virilization to nonclassic CAH in adulthood
  • ☆ Classic CAH
  • Salt Wasting (98% enzyme deficiency):
  • Impaired secretion of both cortisol & aldosterone ⇒↑ ACTH levels + excess adrenal androgen synthesis
  • ▪ Newborns: Vomiting, dehydration, collapse, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia
  • ▪ Females: Ambiguous genitalia at birth (clitoromegaly, labial fusion)
  • ▪ Males: Normal genitalia at birth → but present acutely ill in neonatal period
  • Nonsalt-wasting boys present w/ early genital enlargement, pubarche, and rapid growth.
  • If untreated: Pubic hair, acne, rapid growth, advanced bone age, precocious puberty → very short final height
  • Simple Virilizing (mild enzyme activity, enough aldosterone):
  • Impaired cortisol + ↑ Adrenal androgens
  • ▪ Females: Less severe masculinization
  • ▪ Males: Enlarged phallus
  • Diagnosis: ↑ 17-OH Progesterone (key test) + ↑ ACTH + ↑ Plasma Renin activity + ↓ Cortisol
  • Management: As for acute adrenal crisis & chronic ACI:
  • ☆ Hydrocortisone + Fludrocortisone + Sodium chloride supplements (especially infancy)
  • + Corrective surgery for virilization in females (clitoral reduction, vaginoplasty, labial reconstruction)
  • ☆ Nonclassic CAH (milder deficiency):
  • Glucocorticoids + aldosterone production NORMAL but ↑↑↑ 17OHP so ↑↑↑ Androgens
  • ▪ Girls: Later childhood/adult present w/ hirsutism, acne, premature adrenarche, menstrual irreg, ↓ fertility, PCOS (US)
  • ▪ Males: Asymptomatic
  • Diagnosis: 17-OH Progesterone measurement
  • => ACTH stimulation test:
  • Measure 17OHP 60 min after synthetic ACTH 250 μg admin, an exaggerated rise in 17OHP is seen in nonclassic CAH
  • => Other explorations:
  • ▪ ↑ Testosterone, Androstenedione, DHEAS (in
  • females poorly control CAH)
  • ▪ Genotyping = definitive dg
  • Management:
  • Oral contraceptives (for hirsutism, irregular menses,
  • acne)
  • +/- Prednisolone 2.5-5 mg/day (to normalize
  • ovulatory function)

6. CUSHING'S SYNDROME #5

  • Chronic glucocorticoid excess, whatever the cause. Most common cause = IATROGENIC (chronic glucocorticoid therapy).
  • ● Classification:
  • ☆ ACTH-DEPENDANT (80%) [ACTH HIGH [abnormal secretion ACTH]]:
  • - Cushing Disease (Pituitary adenoma) - 68-80%
  • Most common endogenous cause, Female>> (5:1), 20-40y; mostly MICROADENOMA
  • - Ectopic ACTH Syndrome - 12%
  • Males>> w/ tumors: Carcinoid (lung), Small cell lung cancer, Neuroendocrine tumors (thymus, gut, ovary, pancreas, thyroid
  • C-cells) and common severe hypokalemic alkalosis, that often lack classic Cushingoid features (Poor prognosis)
  • - Ectopic CRH Syndrome (very rare)
  • ☆ ACTH-INDEPENDANT (20%) [ACTH LOW [cortisol excess suppresses pituitary ACTH secretion]]:
  • - Iatrogenic (most common overall)
  • - Adrenal Adenoma (10%) (Secretes usually only cortisol)
  • - Adrenal Carcinoma (8%) (Secretes multiple steroids (cortisol, androgens, aldosterone, estrogens), rapidly progressive,
  • severe w/ HTN & hypokalemia common + Virilization in women)
  • In both adenoma & carcinoma: cortical atrophy of the uninvolved adrenal gld
  • - Nodular adrenal hyperplasia:
  • ▪ Primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease (Carney Complex)
  • ▪ McCune-Albright Syndrome
  • => Carney Complex:
  • Bilateral black & brown pigmented small/normal size adrenal nodules,
  • Myxomas (cardiac, cutaneous, mammary), Spotty skin pigmentation, Endocrine overactivity, sexual precocity, acromegaly,
  • schwannomas.
  • => McCune-Albright Syndrome:
  • Adrenal nodular hyperplasia, Fibrous dysplasia of bone, Café-au-lait skin pigmentation, Precocious puberty
  • ● Clinical features of Cushing's syndrome:
  • Obesity: Truncal, moon facies (75%), buffalo hump, supraclavicular fat pads
  • Skin: Thin, fragile, transparent skin; Facial plethora; Purple striae (abdomen, breasts, hips, thighs); Easy bruising (40%),
  • Acne (glucocorticoid or androgen excess), Hirsutism (80% of females), Hyperpigmentation (only in ectopic ACTH
  • syndrome, NOT in Cushing disease or adrenal tumors)
  • Cardiovascular: HTN (75%), High risk of venous thromboembolism, Peripheral edema, varicose eczema, leg ulcers
  • Mske: Proximal muscle weakness (60%) - MYOPATHY, OSTEOPOROSIS/Osteopenia, Fragility fractures (feet, ribs,
  • vertebrae), Compression fractures (15-20%), Unexplained osteopenia in young/middle-aged adults → evaluate for Cushing's
  • Reproductive:
  • ▪ Females: Oligomenorrhea, amenorrhea, hirsutism, virilization (if androgen excess)
  • ▪ Males: ↓ Libido, impotence, gynecomastia, ↓ body hair, soft testes (cortisol suppresses LH → ↓ testosterone)
  • CNS/Psychological: Emotional lability, anxiety, depression, poor concentration, poor memory, euphoria, severe depression,
  • psychosis, paranoia, Suicide possible
  • Other: IGT/DM (30%), Hyperlipidemia, Renal calculi (hypercalciuria) - 15%, ↑ Susceptibility to infections
  • ● Diagnosis (= Confirming presence of Cushing syndrome + test for its cause)
  • ○ Step 1:
  • DO NOT use random serum cortisol to dg Cushing (limited by episodic secretion & stress), choose one of the following:
  • ☆ 24h Urinary Free Cortisol (UFC) - at least 2 measurements
  • ☆ Late-night Salivary Cortisol - 2 measurements
  • ☆ Low-Dose DST (LDDST) - 2 mg/day for 48 hours (optimal for obesity, alcoholism, psychiatric disorders)
  • [0.5 mg DXM 6-hourly for 48h, measure cortisol at 0 & 48h, Normal cortisol < 1.8 µg/dL]

☆ 1-mg Overnight Dexamethasone Suppression Test (DST) - BEST SCREENING TEST❤️ #6

  • Measure 8AM cortisol →Admin 1 mg dexamethasone (DXM) at 11 PM →Measure 8 AM cortisol next morning→if Cortisol
  • > 1.8 µg/dL (>50 nmol/L), continue investigations w/ 8mg of DXM (inhibition with high dosage of DXM, no "normal ref resp"
  • here)
  • →if Pituitary adenoma secreting ACTH (Cushing DISEASE)→Cortisol will drop >50% of pt’s basal cortisol
  • [Pt w/ basal cortisol of 30mcg/dL, cortisol will then drop to less than 15mcg/dL the day after]
  • →if Adrenal gland adenoma (ACTH INDEP)→ Cortisol will +/- remain the same or diminish but very little
  • →if Ectopic ACTH secretion→ACTH won’t be affected in this case so Cortisol will +/- remain the same
  • →DDX btwn adenoma and ectopic ACTH = ACTH levels (Adenoma = LOW, Ectopic = HIGH)
  • →if suspicion of Cushing DISEASE after DXM test => MRI w/ contrast (to see the pituitary adenoma)
  • ☆ Alternative: Midnight serum cortisol:
  • ▪ Awake midnight plasma cortisol levels > 7.5 µg/dL (200 nmol/L) = highly suggestive of Cushing
  • ▪ Sleeping midnight plasma cortisol levels < 1.8 µg/dL (50 nmol/L) = excludes Cushing's
  • ○ Step 2 (Should actually be done in the first morning, before the DXM test):
  • ☆ Measure 8-9 AM Plasma ACTH:
  • - ACTH < 10 pg/mL = ACTH-INDEPENDENT (low)→ Adrenal tumor (adenoma/carcinoma)→ Abdominal CT (best) or MRI
  • - ACTH > 52 pg/mL OR inappropriately normal = ACTH-DEPENDENT (high)→ Pituitary (Cushing disease) OR Ectopic ACTH
  • [Hence the High-Dose DXM test or Liddle test]
  • ○ Step 3: Imaging
  • → If ACTH-dependent + suppressible on HDDST → Pituitary MRI with gadolinium
  • →If ACTH-dependent + NOT suppressible → CT Chest, Abdomen, Pelvis (search for ectopic tumor)
  • →If ACTH-independent → Abdominal CT/MRI (adrenal tumor)
  • ● Other labs:
  • ↑ DHEA, DHEA-S, Androstenedione
  • ↑ Hb, Ht, RBC (Polythemia)
  • ↓ Lymphocytes, ↓ Eosinophils
  • ☆ Hypokalemic alkalosis (100% in ectopic ACTH and adrenal carcinoma)
  • ☆ Hyperglycemia, DM
  • ☆ ↑ Cholesterol, ↑ Triglycerides
  • ☆ Suppressed TSH, Gonadotropins, GH
  • ● Treatment:
  • ☆ Cushing Disease (Pituitary):
  • 1) Transsphenoidal selective adenectomy (TSS)→if failed TSS or Recurrent disease:
  • 2) Radiation/radiosurgery but may take months-years for cortisol levels to fall so Medical therapy* in the interim
  • 3) Bilateral adrenalectomy (if severe, failed surgery/radiation/medical therapy) and life-long replacement w/
  • glucocorticoids and mineralocorticoids = needed after
  • →Risk: Nelson's syndrome (corticotroph tumor growth + hyperpigmentation after adrenalectomy) but prophylactic
  • radiotherapy reduces Nelson's risk
  • * Medical Therapy:
  • ♡ PASIREOTIDE (somatostatin analog, binds SST5) 0.6-0.9 mg SC BID; normalizes UFC in ~30%; worsens glucose tolerance
  • ♡ CABERGOLINE (dopamine agonist) - 1-7 mg/week; normalizes UFC in 10-30%
  • => Act directly on corticotroph tumors to inhibit ACTH production
  • Alternatives = Steroidogenesis inhibitors: Ketoconazole, Metyrapone

☆ Adrenal Adenoma: Unilateral laparoscopic adrenalectomy - excellent prognosis #7

  • ☆ Adrenal Carcinoma: Surgical excision (rarely curative) + Mitotane (adrenolytic, 6-12 g/d) +/- Ketoconazole/Metyrapone
  • ☆ Ectopic ACTH Syndrome: Localize & resect tumor if possible; Ketoconazole + Metyrapone to control cortisol excess;
  • Severe hypokalemia: K+ replacement + Spironolactone
  • => Bilateral adrenalectomy if tumor not found
  • 7. PRIMARY ALDOSTERONISM
  • Autonomous aldosterone hypersecretion w/ suppressed renin levels. (~10% of hypertensive pt [most common 2° HTN])
  • (DDX Secondary hyperaldosteronism = aldosterone hypersecretion 2° to high circulating renin levels)
  • ● Subtypes:
  • ▪ Bilateral Idiopathic Hyperaldosteronism (IHA) - 60% (macro/micronodular adrenal hyperplasia)
  • ▪ Aldosterone-Producing Adenoma (APA) - 35% (< 2.5 cm) (=Conn’s syndr)
  • ▪ Adrenal Carcinoma - < 1% (rare)
  • ● Screening indications:
  • - Resistant HTN (not controlled on 3 agents) or Stage 2-3 HTN (BP > 160-179 / 100-109)
  • - HTN + HYPOK+ (K+ < 3.7) - spontaneous or thiazide-induced
  • - HTN developing before 40y
  • - Adrenal incidentaloma
  • - When considering 2° HTN
  • ● Clinical Features:
  • HTN (often severe), HYPOK+ (only 40% have low K+: NORMAL K+ DOES NOT EXCLUDE DIAGNOSIS),
  • Polyuria (from hypokalemia), Muscle weakness, cramping, tetany, periodic paralysis, Mild metabolic alkalosis
  • IMPORTANT: Hypokalemia in a hypertensive pt NOT on diuretics → mineralocorticoid excess until proven otherwise.
  • ● Diagnostic Workup: 1) Case-detection tests, 2) Confirmatory studies, 3) Subtypes evaluation tests
  • Step 1: Aldosterone excess identification
  • - Morning (8-10 AM) ambulatory paired measure of Plasma Aldosterone Concentration (PAC) + Plasma Renin Activity (PRA)
  • ☆ Calculate Aldosterone:Renin Ratio (ARR) = PAC/PRA (should be carried out in the normokalemic situation)
  • => Ratio > 20 (ng/dL) + PAC ≥ 15 ng/dL = HIGHLY SUGGESTIVE
  • => Normal or ↑ Renin = EXCLUDES primary aldosteronism
  • => ↑ PAC + ↑ PRA with ARR < 10 = SECONDARY aldosteronism
  • ⚠️ Medications to STOP 4 weeks before testing: Spironolactone, Eplerenone & Beta-blockers (↓ renin)
  • → Control BP w/ Doxazosin or CCBs
  • Step 2: Confirmatory tests: Demonstrate lack of aldosterone suppressibility w/ sodium or volume loading
  • Step 3: Subtype evaluation
  • ▪ Adrenal CT: APA = hypodense nodule < 2 cm BUT incidentalomas are common with age → AVS if in doubt
  • ▪ Adrenal Venous Sampling (AVS): GOLD STANDARD for DDX unilateral (APA) from bilateral (IHA) disease
  • → Measure aldosterone from both adrenal veins to obtain a gradient. Do ONLY if surgery is feasible and desired.
  • ● Treatment:
  • - Surgery (for APA/Unilateral disease): Unilateral laparoscopic adrenalectomy - tx of choice; low morbidity
  • - Medical Therapy (for IHA/Bilateral disease OR patients unfit for surgery):
  • ☆ Spironolactone (50-400 mg/day), monitor K+ & BP, SE: Gynecomastia, impotence, menstrual irreg (androgen/
  • progesterone R interaction) OR Eplerenone (50-200 mg/day, BID) - selective mineralocorticoid antagonist
  • Other antihypertensives: Amiloride, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, CCBs, Thiazides

8. PHEOCHROMOCYTOMA & PARAGANGLIOMA (PPGL) #8

  • ☆ Pheochromocytoma (PCA)= Chromaffin tumor of adrenal medulla, secretes catecholamines: Epi/Norepi (cst/episodic)
  • ☆ Paraganglioma (PGL)= Extra-adrenal chromaffin tumor
  • - Sympathetic PGL (non head-neck): Prevertebral, paravertebral, thoracoabdominal, pelvis, organ of Zuckerkandl -
  • functional (secrete catecholamines, mainly norepinephrine bc lack PMNT)
  • - Parasympathetic PGL: Head and neck (close to major arteries and nerves) - usually nonfunctional (no catecholamines or
  • only dopamine
  • [rare, more likely
  • malignant])
  • Epidemiology: Rare, 10% bilateral, 10% familial, 15-20% malignant
  • ● Screening indications:
  • ▪ Genetic mutation carriers or family history of MEN2, VHL2, NF-1, SDHx mutations
  • ▪ Young hypertensive patients, severe/resistant HTN (paroxysmal or sustained)
  • ▪ Hypertensive crisis during anesthesia/surgery
  • ▪ Headaches, Diaphoresis, Palpitations, or tachycardia, episodic anxiety, tremor (40%), abdominal/chest pain (in HTN pt)
  • ▪ Adrenal incidentaloma
  • ● Clinical Features:
  • HTN (sustained or episodic, often resistant) + Orthostatic hypotension
  • Classic triad: Headache, Diaphoresis, Palpitations/Tachycardia
  • ▪ Pallor or flushing, livedo reticularis, anxiety, visual disturbance, seizures, dyspnea, weight loss
  • ▪ Hyperglycemia/DM
  • ▪ Features of associated genetic conditions
  • ● Complications:
  • ▪ Cardiovascular: LV failure, dilated cardiomyopathy (reversible), dysrhythmias
  • ▪ Respiratory: Pulmonary edema
  • ▪ Metabolic: Carbohydrate intolerance, hypercalcemia
  • ▪ Neurological: Cerebrovascu, hypertensive encephalopathy
  • ● Biochemical Diagnosis - BEST TESTS (most sensitive):
  • ☆ Plasma Free Metanephrines (most sensitive) / ☆ Urinary Fractionated Metanephrines (when plasma values =borderline)
  • Why metanephrines?
  • Catecholamines are secreted intermittently but metanephrines = continuously produced by COMT in tumor cells and leak
  • directly into circulation
  • => Elevated metanephrine → likely adrenal pheochromocytoma (paragangliomas lack PNMT, don't make them)
  • • If both biochemical tests are borderline: Clonidine Suppression Test (but offers little advantage & potentially dangerous)
  • • Test for non-secretory tumors: Serum Chromogranin A (CgA) - useful for non-secretory PGLs
  • ● Localization (ONLY after biochemical confirmation):
  • 1. CT Abdomen/Pelvis (w/ nonionic contrast) - first choice
  • 2. MRI - for adrenal pheochromocytoma, skull base/neck PGLs, metastases (bright T2 hyperintense)
  • 3. 123 I-MIBG Scintigraphy - for metastatic PPGLs detected by other imaging modalities
  • 4. PET/CT - more sensitive, especially for metastatic disease

● Genetic Testing indicated for: #9

  • Bilateral tumors, Extra-adrenal localization, Malignant tumor, (+) fam hx, Syndromic presentation, Young age at diagnosis
  • All patients should be engaged in shared decision-making about genetic testing
  • ● Management: ☆ Surgery
  • - Laparoscopic: Small, benign, apparently noninvasive tumors
  • OR Open resection: Large (> 6 cm), invasive, or most PGLs
  • Malignancy: 15-20% are malignant, No reliable histologic markers; malignancy defined by metastasis (not local invasion)
  • ● Perioperative Management (CRITICAL): ❤️
  • Preoperative Preparation (start 7-14 days before surgery):
  • 1) α-blockers FIRST (prevents hypertensive crisis):
  • ☆ Phenoxybenzamine (nonselective) - 10 mg BID OR ☆ Doxazosin (α1-selective) - 2-16 mg/day
  • Goal= BP ≤ 130/85 mmHg without symptomatic orthostasis + ensure adequate hydration
  • 2) Add CCBs if needed (Nicardipine, Nifedipine, Amlodipine) - especially for those who dvp severe orthostatic hypotension
  • with α-adrenergic receptor blockers
  • 3) β-blockers (Propranolol, Atenolol) ONLY AFTER α-blockade 3-4 days later - to control tachycardia
  • NEVER use β-blockers without α-blockade (risk of unopposed α-stimulation → hypertensive crisis)

9. KEY DRUGS TO REMEMBER (ADRENAL PHARMACOLOGY) #10

  • Drug Mechanism Use
  • Hydrocortisone Glucocorticoid replacement ACI, CAH, Adrenal crisis
  • Fludrocortisone Mineralocorticoid ACI, CAH
  • replacement
  • Prednisone/Prednisolone Synthetic glucocorticoid ACI (alternative), CAH (nonclassic)
  • Spironolactone Mineralocorticoid receptor Primary aldosteronism (IHA)
  • antagonist
  • Eplerenone Selective mineralocorticoid Primary aldosteronism (IHA)
  • receptor antagonist
  • Ketoconazole Inhibits steroidogenesis Cushing's (medical therapy)
  • Metyrapone Inhibits 11β-hydroxylase Cushing's (medical therapy)
  • Mitotane Adrenolytic Adrenal carcinoma
  • Pasireotide Somatostatin analog Cushing DISEASE
  • (SST5)
  • Cabergoline Dopamine agonist Cushing DISEASE
  • Mifepristone USA
  • Phenoxybenzamine Nonselective α-blocker Pheochromocytoma (preop)
  • Doxazosin α1-selective blocker Pheochromocytoma (preop)
